Zayed International Airport (AUH), formerly Abu Dhabi International Airport, is the primary aviation gateway for the capital of the United Arab Emirates. It is a major hub for Etihad Airways and serves millions of passengers annually with connections to destinations across the globe. Historical Background and Origins The history of civil aviation in Abu Dhabi dates back to the late 1960s, when Al Bateen Airport was established as the first international airport under the initiative of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. Construction began in 1966, and the airport was officially opened in 1970, but it quickly became insufficient due to rapidly growing air traffic . By the mid-1970s, planning for a larger airport began. The current site, located about 15 kilometers from Al Bateen, was selected, and construction started in 1977. The new Abu Dhabi International Airport was inaugurated on January 2, 1982, replacing Al Bateen as the main international facility 2 1 . Over the years, the airport expanded with multiple terminals to accommodate increasing passenger numbers. Terminal Overview Current Terminal Status As of late 2023, Zayed International Airport has consolidated its operations into a single main terminal: Terminal A (formerly known as the Midfield Terminal) . Terminal A is now the only operational terminal for all international flights. The previous Terminals 1, 2, and 3 have been closed or are used only as standby facilities . The terminal features a distinctive X-shaped design, which optimizes passenger flow and operational efficiency . It serves the northernmost emirate of the United Arab Emirates, handling a mix of regional passenger flights from airlines such as Air Arabia and SalamAir, along with cargo and charter operations. While smaller than the mega-hubs of Dubai and Abu Dhabi, the airport offers a stress-free entry point to a part of the UAE that rewards visitors with mountains, desert, and a slower pace of life. Getting There Reaching Ras Al Khaimah International Airport is straightforward from within the emirate and from neighbouring emirates. From Ras Al Khaimah City: The airport is about a 25-minute drive from the city centre, depending on traffic. Taxis are readily available from hotels and the city centre; the fare typically ranges from AED 50 to AED 70. There is no direct public bus to the terminal, but the Ras Al Khaimah Transport Authority operates a bus service (route 9) that stops at Al Hamra Mall, about 3 kilometres from the airport. From there, a short taxi ride completes the journey. From Dubai: The drive takes approximately 1.5 hours via the E311 (Emirates Road) or E18, with the latter offering a more scenic coastal route. Car rental companies operate from the airport, including Thrifty and Budget, though it is advisable to book ahead during peak seasons. Alternatively, shared shuttle services and private transfers are available from Dubai hotels, costing around AED 250–400 per person. From other Northern Emirates: Ajman and Umm Al Quwain are within 30–50 minutes by car; Sharjah is about 70 minutes. Parking at the airport is free for the first hour and thereafter costs AED 10 per hour or AED 50 per day, with separate short-term and long-term lots. Inside the Terminal The terminal is compact and easy to navigate. On departure, check-in counters are located on the ground floor, with security screening immediately after. The security area is efficient, and most passengers clear it within 10–15 minutes during quiet periods. The departure lounge, located on the first floor, offers views of the tarmac and a small selection of shops and cafes. Facilities confirmed at the airport include wheelchair-accessible entrances, toilets, and car parks, as well as a changing table in the accessible restroom. Baggage storage is available for a fee—ideal for passengers with layovers or early arrivals. The terminal also features a prayer room and free Wi-Fi throughout. Passengers should note that the airport does not operate 24 hours a day; it typically opens several hours before the first flight and closes after the last arrival. Busiest times are weekday evenings (Monday–Thursday around 10–11 pm), when check-in and security queues can lengthen. Arriving two hours before a scheduled flight is sufficient, but an extra 30 minutes is wise during peak periods. There are no airline lounges at present, but the terminal’s size means gate-to-gate walking time is under 10 minutes. Food options are limited: a cafe serving snacks and beverages, and vending machines. For a full meal, passengers are better off eating at the airport’s on-site restaurant (near check-in) or bringing their own provisions. Ras Al Khaimah International Airport and the Region Ras Al Khaimah is often overshadowed by its flashy neighbours, but this emirate has its own distinct character. Geographically, it is the most mountainous of the UAE, with the Hajar range rising dramatically behind the coast. Jebel Jais, the country’s highest peak at 1,934 metres, is less than an hour from the airport. Here, adventure tourists flock to the world’s longest zipline and the Via Ferrata climbing routes, while the Jais Rook Restaurant offers panoramic views over the Persian Gulf. For those seeking culture, the old town of Ras Al Khaimah features the National Museum, housed in a 18th-century fort, and the Dhayah Fort, a hilltop defensive structure that saw conflict in the 19th century. The emirate’s history as a pearl-diving centre is preserved in the Al Jazirah Al Hamra Heritage Village, an abandoned pearling town with coral-block houses. Nature lovers can explore the mangroves of Al Suwaidi, home to flamingos and herons, or take a desert safari into the Rub’ al Khali near the border with Oman. The emirate also boasts kilometres of relatively undeveloped beaches, from Al Marjan Island’s resort-lined coast to the quieter stretches near Rams. Why do people come here? Some are attracted by the luxury all-inclusives of Waldorf Astoria and Ritz-Carlton, others by the affordability compared to Dubai. Business travellers use RAK for the growing industrial zones and free zones. Increasingly, the airport serves as a alternative for visitors to the northern emirates, particularly those heading to the Hajar mountains or the coast. One thing to keep in mind: Ras Al Khaimah is still less internationalised than Dubai. English is widely spoken, but some taxi drivers and shopkeepers appreciate basic Arabic greetings. Alcohol is available in hotel restaurants and bars, but not in supermarkets. Fridays and Saturdays are the weekend; Sundays are regular working days. Practical Information Operating Hours: The airport is not open 24 hours. It opens approximately three hours before the first scheduled flight and closes after the last arrival. Check flight timings to ensure the terminal is open. Contact: +971 7 207 5200; website: http://www.rakairport.com/ Baggage Storage: Available at the check-in hall; cost around AED 30 per item per day. Accessibility: Fully wheelchair-accessible, with adapted toilets and parking bays. Parking: Short-term (first hour free, then AED 10/hour) and long-term (AED 50/day). Tips: If your flight departs during the busiest window (10–11 pm), arrive an extra 30 minutes early and consider booking a taxi in advance, as ride-hail apps may have surge pricing. For early morning flights, note that the terminal opens only an hour or two before departure—do not expect to wait inside if you arrive too early. One concrete piece of advice: Because the airport lacks a wide range of shops and eateries, pick up food, water, and any essentials in town before heading to the terminal, especially if you have a late-evening flight when the cafe may be closed. In Punjab, Amritsar, Jalandhar, Ludhiana, Mandi Gobindgarh and Chandigarh produce a large volume of cargo. Rail Connectivity The port can handle incoming and outgoing trains simultaneously, with several railway sidings to support loading and offloading. APM Terminals Pipavav was the first port in India to receive double stacked container trains in March 2006. Located immediately west of the centre of Kuwait City , it lies on the southern shores of Kuwait Bay off the Persian Gulf . The Kuwait Ports Authority [ ar ] manages and operates the Port of Shuwaikh. The Port of Shuwaikh serves ocean-going vessels at its deep-water berths, and it has ample modern container facilities. It is the country's most important commercial port and covers 320 hectares of land and 120 hectares of water surface. The Navigation Channel inside Kuwait Bay is dredged to a depth of 8.5 meters (minimum tide level), and it is about eight kilometers long. At any tide, the Port of Shuwaikh can receive vessels to 7.5 meters draft. At high tide, vessels to 9.5 meters draft can enter and leave the Port of Shuwaikh. The Port of Shuwaikh contains 21 berths with a total length of 4055 meters. Fourteen of the berths have a depth of 10 meters, four are 8.5 meters deep, and three have alongside depth of 6.7 meters. Cargo vessels travelling through the Port of Shuwaikh include merchant ships and other vessels that include liners, tramps, fishing trawlers, and small passenger ships as well as cargo-laden container and roll-on/roll-off vessels and barges. The Main Terminal handles every scheduled domestic and international flight. The Aramco Terminal is closed to the public. The Royal Terminal is closed to almost everybody. IATA CODE DMM ICAO CODE OEDF MAIN TERMINAL Six storeys, 327,000 m² TERMINALS OPEN TO YOU One of three On this page The three terminals → Inside the Main Terminal → DMM and OEDF codes → Three buildings · one you can walk into The three terminals The Main Terminal This is the terminal every passenger means when they say Dammam Airport. It is a six-storey building of 327,000 square metres, and it handles domestic and international flights under one roof, with separate halls rather than separate buildings. Saudia, Flynas and Flyadeal carry most of the domestic traffic. International carriers work the same terminal, with Dubai the busiest route on the board at around seventy flights a week. The full list of destinations, with the airlines on each one, is on the nonstop route table . Main terminal of King Fahd International Airport, Saudi Arabia. The map covers the departures concourse and the landside kerb. Gates 15 to 27 run along a single finger with aircraft parked on the apron beside it, and the icons mark the lounges, food outlets, shops, baggage reclaim belts, information desk and car hire counters along the way. On the landside edge, the pick-up and drop-off lane sits between the taxi ranks and the bus stops, with the car park behind them, which is the sequence to expect when you walk out of arrivals. The full airport, including the aprons and both runways, is on the wider airport map . The Aramco Terminal Saudi Aramco runs its own air operation from its own terminal at King Fahd, and it is not open to the public. The airline is Saudi Aramco Aviation, operating as Mukamalah. It exists to move Aramco employees and contractors between Dammam and the company’s remote sites: Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, Tanajib in the north east, and Shaybah deep in the Empty Quarter. These are places with no useful commercial service, which is why a private oil company ended up running a scheduled airline. Two things follow from that, and both catch people out. You cannot buy a ticket on an Aramco flight, and arriving at the Aramco Terminal without a company badge or a sponsored booking will not get you airside. And a search for “Aramco airport” in the Eastern Province usually means King Fahd itself rather than the terminal, because locals have used the name for the whole airport for decades. If you are flying Aramco, your departure point is the Aramco Terminal, not the Main Terminal, and the two are separate buildings on an enormous site. Confirm which one before you set off. The Royal Terminal Reserved for the Saudi royal family, senior government officials and visiting heads of state. It covers around 16,400 square metres and has four of its own boarding bridges. It sees very little use. Its aircraft stands are counted among the airport’s thirty remote positions, which is the only way most passengers will ever encounter it: as a set of parked aircraft seen from a taxiway. Arrival · Departure · Boarding · Mezzanine · Service Inside the Main Terminal The airport names its levels rather than numbering them, and the signage uses the same words: Arrival, Departure, Boarding, Mezzanine and Service. Directions below follow those names. Eating, shopping and lounges Food and coffee run around the clock, which is unusual for an airport this size, and the duty-free store operates on both the departures and the arrivals levels. The outlets, the queue to plan for and the arrivals purchase limits are set out in the guide to duty free and eating at the airport . Four lounges operate here, two on the international side and two domestic, and access is sold at the door as well as through membership schemes. Prayer rooms and the mosque The mosque is not inside the terminal. It sits above the multistorey car park and holds around 2,000 worshippers, with enclosed air-conditioned walkways connecting it to the building, so reaching it does not mean going outside. Inside the terminal there are prayer rooms on every level, each with ablution facilities, and they stay open around the clock. The airport publishes their exact positions as a layer on its own terminal map, which is worth using rather than a list, because the layout shifts with construction work. Wi-Fi and phone service Free Wi-Fi covers the terminal. The network is DAMMAM AIRPORT FREE WIFI and the password is DAMMAM123. It carries browsing and messaging; anything heavier is unreliable at a busy hour. Telecom desks in the terminal sell local SIM cards and handle top-ups and roaming. For a stay of more than a day or two in the Eastern Province that is the steadier option. Banks, ATMs and currency Banks and cash machines appear as their own layer on the terminal map, and currency exchange counters sit landside. Alinma Bank is on the departure level, beside the Plaza Premium lounge. If you are bringing cash rather than withdrawing it, the amount you may carry without declaring it is set by customs rather than by the airport. Smoking Smoking is confined to designated smoking rooms in the departures area. Nowhere else in the terminal allows it, and the same restriction covers vapes, because Saudi law treats nicotine e-cigarettes as tobacco products when deciding where they may be used. The Plaza Premium lounge has a smoking room of its own. Getting in and out The covered car park connects to the terminal by walkway, and taxis, ride-hailing and SAPTCO buses all work the kerb outside. Arriving passengers clear passport control, collect bags, then pass customs into the arrivals hall. Times on the board move. Check live arrivals before setting out to meet anyone. One for your ticket, one for the cockpit Dammam Airport Code: DMM and OEDF The IATA code for King Fahd International Airport is DMM. The ICAO code is OEDF. DMM is the three-letter code on your ticket, your boarding pass and your baggage tags. OEDF is the four-letter code used in flight plans and by air traffic control, and it follows the regional pattern: OE for Saudi Arabia, DF for this airport. Passengers never need it, but it is what appears on tracking sites and in cockpit paperwork. Before you arrive Frequently Asked Questions How many terminals does Dammam Airport have? There is also a mosque holding about 2,000, reached by air-conditioned walkway from the terminal, which sits above the car park rather than inside the building. Can you smoke at Dammam Airport? Only in the designated smoking rooms in departures. The rest of the terminal is non-smoking, and vapes are treated the same way under Saudi law, so there is no separate allowance for them.
